h: An emptying Parliament: when debate itself is called obstruction
dek: Swarati Sabhapandit writes that the government is wiping out the very legitimacy of parliamentary deliberation by calling it a roadblock on the path of its mandate.
body: According to Swarati Sabhapandit, who teaches at Azim Premji University, the Indian Parliament is slowly turning into a place where decisions are made elsewhere and the House merely stamps them. Data from PRS Legislative Research shows that in the 17th Lok Sabha (2019-24), at least 35 percent of bills were passed with less than an hour of debate.

The first Lok Sabha sat for an average of 135 days a year; in the 17th this fell to 55. In the 14th and 15th Lok Sabha, more than 70 percent of bills were sent to parliamentary committees; in the 17th this dropped to less than 15 percent. The writer points out that laws with far-reaching effects, such as the 2019 UAPA amendment, the Citizenship Amendment Act, the 2020 FCRA amendment and the three farm laws, were passed without close scrutiny. In 2016 the Aadhaar Act was made a money bill and so kept away from the Rajya Sabha.

She believes this decline is not new: the Emergency and the 42nd Amendment, the 1985 anti-defection law that handed the power of debate to party offices, the criminalisation of politics and the post-1991 era all played a part. But the difference now is that the rules are not just being broken, they are being called meaningless. At the start of the winter session in December 2025, the ruling leader described Parliament as a place for 'delivery, not drama'.

According to the writer, once an election mandate is taken as reason enough to avoid debate, every question from the Opposition starts to look like obstruction. This article first appeared in the University of Pennsylvania's 'India in Transition'.
nazar: This analysis comes in the very week a constitution-changing bill like delimitation is being brought in a special session with no Question Hour and no Zero Hour. The laws that hit minorities, farmers and civil society groups first were all products of this same haste. Debate is not the noise of democracy, it is its breath.
sawal: Who will answer for the laws passed without committee scrutiny?
ref: Money bill
A bill on which the Rajya Sabha can only make suggestions and cannot block; it is certified by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
ank: Bills passed with less than an hour of debate
Sitting days a year in the 17th Lok Sabha

h: First the Election Commission's credibility, then delimitation
dek: M.K. Venu writes that when the voter rolls themselves are in question, regional parties backing the delimitation bill would be suicidal for multi-party democracy.
body: A four-day special session of Parliament has been called from 30 November, in which the delimitation bill is to be brought. M.K. Venu, founding editor of The Wire, accepts that the population has grown since the 1971 census and that more seats may be needed. But this is happening at a time when the Election Commission is accused of cutting names from the voter rolls on a large scale and the Supreme Court is repeatedly making it reverse its steps.

The writer asks regional parties to set conditions before giving any support: the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, a rebuilding of the Commission, a change in how appointments are made, and an end to the permanent legal immunity given to the commissioners. He tells Sharad Pawar's NCP and M.K. Stalin's DMK in particular that letting the bill pass while ignoring the wreckage of the voter rolls would be fatal for them.

According to Venu, the BJP's aim is one-party rule: the 'Congress-mukt Bharat' (Congress-free India) of 2014 has become an 'Opposition-free India' after 2024. He fears that once the bill passes, Gyanesh Kumar will become an ex officio member of the Delimitation Commission and the maps will be drawn the way they were in Assam and Jammu and Kashmir, where there were charges of gerrymandering.

The article's last argument is about the mood of the country. The writer says Gen Z protests across the country have shown that the game of making power permanent has a shelf life. The gap between Parliament and the people is growing, and a bill pushed through by force could give birth to a bigger mass movement than any so far.
nazar: Delimitation is not a technical sum, it is a question of how power is shared. Handing the maps of constituencies for the next twenty-five years to the very body accused of cutting crores of voters' names will deepen the lack of trust. The strength of the article is that it asks for a fair referee before the seats are counted.
sawal: How can a commission nobody trusts draw the maps?
ref: Gerrymandering
Drawing the boundaries of constituencies so that a particular party or community gains or loses.
photo_note: Representational image: an instrument at Jantar Mantar

h: Sanctions on settlers, a free pass for the Israeli state
dek: Yara Hawari writes that Western sanctions target a few settler groups and so shield the state machinery that runs the occupation.
body: On 17 November, at al-Duyuk al-Tahta on the outskirts of Jericho, 72-year-old Palestinian woman Fadda Fuhaidat was shot in the head outside her home. Settlers had recently driven out at least 13 Palestinian families there. Yara Hawari, co-director of the Palestinian policy network Al-Shabaka, says that a few hours after the killing, Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich arrived at the new outpost and praised the settlers.

Jericho is the same city that was the first to be handed to the Palestinian Authority under the 1994 Oslo Accords. According to the writer, this is the first settlement built inside a Palestinian city since Hebron almost five decades ago. The takeover was led by the Nachala organisation, founded by Daniella Weiss, with the support of the Binyamin Regional Council.

Since the Gaza war began, more than 6,000 Palestinians in the West Bank, half of them children, have been forcibly displaced. In January and February 2025 the army emptied the refugee camps of Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarm, leaving about 33,000 people homeless. Hawari says settlers and the army work together, and the settlements survive on Israeli-only roads, water and power networks, and government subsidies.

Britain, Australia, Canada and the European Union have imposed asset freezes and travel bans on Nachala and Weiss. According to the writer, this lets governments look as if they are doing something, but the effect is small; Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong's statement did not even mention the Israeli government. She says sanctions should fall on the whole colonial structure, but for now no one seems to have the courage for that.
nazar: It is convenient to single out a few 'bad' settlers, because it makes the occupation look like the work of a handful of extremists rather than the policy of a state. When a minister himself turns up at the new outpost to cheer, that distinction does not hold. Accountability must be fixed where the decisions and the money are.
sawal: Why do Western sanctions not fall on ministers like Smotrich?
ref: Oslo Accords
The 1993-95 Israel-Palestine agreements that created the Palestinian Authority and gave limited self-rule in parts of the West Bank.

h: Nuclear weapons: abolition or catastrophe, there is no middle road
dek: Melissa Parke writes that the Trump, Putin and Xi meeting repeated old lines, while the real path is the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons.
body: According to Melissa Parke, executive director of the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons (ICAN), the world today faces its biggest nuclear danger since the Cold War. In the early 1990s, when only five countries had these weapons, the US and Russia had a chance to get rid of them, and it was lost.

Today these two countries hold about 90 percent of the world's nuclear weapons, and both have waged wars against countries without nuclear weapons, Ukraine and Iran. The writer says both Putin and Trump have threatened nuclear use. The first three-way meeting of Trump, Putin and Xi Jinping repeated that a nuclear war cannot be won, but nothing new came out of it beyond the old talk of reducing risk and stopping proliferation.

Parke sees 'deterrence', the theory of preventing war through fear, as a guess about human behaviour with no evidence behind it. Nine countries and their allies have about 4,000 weapons that can be launched at short notice.

As an alternative she points to the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, which 101 countries have signed or ratified. Its first review meeting is to be held in New York under South Africa's presidency, while this same year the review of the Non-Proliferation Treaty ended without agreement for the third time in a row. South Africa is itself an example: in the 1990s it destroyed its nuclear weapons under international monitoring.
nazar: India and Pakistan are both among the nine countries outside this treaty, and with every bout of tension between them the language of nuclear threats returns. For peace in South Asia, this debate is not a distant one. For countries that claim to lead the Global South, standing with the 101 should come naturally.
sawal: Will India attend the review meeting of the nuclear weapons ban treaty?
ref: Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW)
A treaty adopted at the United Nations in 2017 that fully bans making, keeping and using nuclear weapons.

h: More loans, fewer women borrowers
dek: Samia Saliq shows that in Pakistan farm credit to women doubled, and yet the number of women borrowers fell.
body: Sakina started selling milk from a single cow she got from her father. In three years she has four animals and more than 40 customers. Her husband delivers the milk, and the account book is in his name too. When Sakina asked a bank for a loan for two more cows, the bank said no, because her name was nowhere in years of sales records.

Samia Saliq, who leads work on women's economic and digital inclusion at Karandaaz Pakistan, sets out State Bank figures: farm credit to women rose from Rs 44 billion in 2021 to Rs 105 billion in 2025, but in the same period women borrowers fell from 436,000 to 377,000, a drop of about 14 percent. Banks are meeting targets by giving more money to their old customers.

Farming makes up about 23 percent of Pakistan's GDP, and nearly two-thirds of that is livestock. Six of every ten working women are in farming, forestry or fishing. The writer says that unless banks understand the difference between a woman who earns wages, one who rears the family's animals unpaid, and one like Sakina who runs a business, they cannot assess them properly.

She gives the example of dairy cooperatives in Kenya, where milk suppliers got advances based on digital records. Her suggestion is that the provincial livestock department link milk buyers and banks, that each woman's supply and payment be recorded, that the money come into her own account, and that the State Bank publish the real number of women borrowers along with the loan amounts.
nazar: This article shows how shiny figures can hide the truth: the money grew but the women shrank. In India too, self-help groups and Mudra loans are often praised by the amount, not by asking who controls the money. Only when the woman's name is in the account book will her work be counted.
sawal: Why don't India's banks publish the real number of women borrowers?
ref: Banking on Equality
A State Bank of Pakistan policy that aims to double credit to women in priority sectors by 2028.

h: Spain's election: a tenants' movement and a scattered Left
dek: Carlos Delclós writes that housing is the biggest issue before the 29 November election, but the party that gave voice to this unrest has grown weak.
body: On 23 September, in Madrid's Retiro district, 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who is disabled and had lived there since 1956, was carried out of her home on a stretcher. Police broke the human chain formed by neighbours and the tenants' union. Two weeks later she died in hospital. Protests followed in about forty cities, and tents went up in Puerta del Sol, the square of the 2011 Indignados movement.

Carlos Delclós, who teaches sociology at the Autonomous University of Barcelona, explains that on 2 October the PP, Vox and Junts struck down two emergency housing decrees of Pedro Sánchez's government, after which a snap election was called. Rents are at a record high; only 14.5 percent of Spaniards aged 16 to 29 manage to live apart from their parents. In the official survey in October, housing came out as the biggest worry, even among right-wing voters.

Under Sánchez the minimum wage rose by more than 60 percent, temporary contracts fell, undocumented migrants got a path to legal status, and abroad there were steps like recognising Palestine and an arms embargo on Israel. Even so, polls show a PP-Vox majority. According to the writer, the political cycle that began in 2011 seems to be ending: Podemos, Sumar and Ada Colau's Frente Amplio have split from one another, and parties built on their leaders' image could not go further than them.

The new generation is organising in tenants' unions rather than parties. On 11 November came the first general strike in fourteen years, which began from a demand of the tenants' unions. The writer concludes that whoever forms the government will have to face a fighting housing movement with its own programme.
nazar: Spain's story is a familiar one: the real issue is on the street, but the forces that should raise it in Parliament are scattered, and the far Right moves into that empty space. In Indian cities too, rents, evictions and bulldozers are shaping ordinary people's lives. The answer is a movement that treats housing as a right, not the image of some leader.
sawal: Can tenants' unions stop the far Right in Spain?
ref: Indignados
Spain's 2011 youth movement that occupied squares against unemployment and austerity cuts; the Podemos party grew out of it.

h: Pakistan's Gen Z: hardship is heavy, yet the streets are silent
dek: Nazir Ahmed Arijo asks why Pakistan's young people have not risen up despite an economy worse than its neighbours', and how long this silence will last.
body: In Nepal and Bangladesh, young people shook governments over rising prices, joblessness and inequality. Independent writer Nazir Ahmed Arijo asks why, when Pakistan's economy is worse than theirs, no such anger is seen there. By the World Bank's new poverty line of 4.20 dollars a day, the writer says, 44.7 percent of Pakistanis live in poverty.

According to Arijo, big businessmen, bureaucrats and those in power have piled up enough for three generations to live in comfort, and skilled and wealthy people are leaving the country. The middle class still has enough buying power to stay quiet. But because government schools are in a bad state, even salaried families are struggling with private school fees, and the shutdown of industry is hitting the young hardest.

The writer sees the campaign to create new provinces in the same light, calling it a 'divide and rule' move by the elite. No lessons were learnt from the disputes over the Kalabagh dam and the Cholistan canal, and Sindh sees this as a threat to its land, identity and culture. Many legal experts, including former Senate chairman Raza Rabbani, say a referendum cannot replace Article 239(4) of the Constitution.

Arijo suggests real political and financial decentralisation, a clear sharing of power, a stronger Parliament and democracy inside parties, so that merit, not money or family, decides who rises. Otherwise, he warns, the pent-up restlessness of the young could turn into a nationwide movement.
nazar: Mistaking silence for contentment is an old error of every ruler. Kathmandu and Dhaka showed that when the young see no way forward within the system, anger erupts suddenly. Pakistan's rulers should focus on jobs, schools and democratic participation instead of redrawing provincial lines; that is the plain lesson of this article.
sawal: How long will Pakistan's middle class stay quiet?
ref: Gen Z movements
Protests led by the generation born between 1997 and 2012, which recently brought down governments in Nepal and Bangladesh.

h: Former CJI Gavai: one community favoured in judges' appointments
dek: B.R. Gavai has written to the President alleging that Dalits, Adivasis (indigenous communities), backward classes, minorities and women are being left behind in the collegium's recent recommendations.
body: Former Chief Justice of India B.R. Gavai has written to President Droupadi Murmu, raising concern that diversity and merit are being ignored in the appointment and transfer of judges. He alleges that recent collegium recommendations are favouring one particular community. According to him, a community that makes up less than five percent of the population has recently held more than 40 percent of the seats in the Supreme Court. He has asked the President to step in.

Gavai cited Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal's reply in the Rajya Sabha in March 2025. Of the 715 High Court judges appointed since 2018, 22 were Scheduled Caste, 16 Scheduled Tribe, 89 OBC and 37 from minorities, which means nearly three of every four were from the general category. Between January 2021 and January 2026, the share of upper castes was about 80 percent, while OBCs got less than 14 percent of the places.

He wrote that during his own term he had tried for a balanced representation of every section, even the upper castes, and that he is not against any class. Giving examples such as a High Court chief justice being transferred to a smaller High Court and then recommended for a bigger one, he asked whether merit had been ignored in these decisions.
nazar: This complaint does not come from an outside critic but from the man who headed the collegium only a short while ago and who himself comes from the Dalit community. The figures show how far the higher courts are from the social make-up of the country. For a judiciary that guards equality, transparency and diversity in its own appointments are no longer questions that can be put off.
sawal: Why doesn't the collegium make the social data of its recommendations public?
ref: Collegium
The group of the Chief Justice of India and senior Supreme Court judges that recommends the appointment and transfer of judges in the higher courts.

h: Victims must be heard before remission: Supreme Court
dek: Setting aside Anand Mohan's release, the court said that a convict's early release is not just a matter between the government and the convict.
body: The Supreme Court has said that before deciding on a convict's premature release or remission, the government must give the victim or their legal representative a fair chance to be heard, provided the victim can be identified and reached. A bench of Justice Dipankar Datta and Justice Sheel Nagu said this while setting aside the release of former Bihar MP Anand Mohan, who was convicted in the 1994 murder of an IAS officer.

According to the court, the victim's role does not end with the trial and the sentence. The victim is heard in bail and appeals, so leaving them out at the time of release leaves that participation incomplete. The bench also said that Section 473 of the new Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita has no provision for such a hearing either, which shrinks the whole matter of remission to one between the government and the convict.

The court made clear that the victim gets no veto; the final decision will be made by the competent authority according to law and policy. But the victim's objections, such as fear of threats or the lasting effect of the crime, must be weighed in the decision. The bench relied on the Jagjeet Singh vs Ashish Mishra judgment for this.
nazar: After the release of the men convicted in the Bilkis Bano case, the question came up again and again that no one had even asked those who suffered the crime. This judgment fills that gap. Especially for victims from weaker sections, whose offenders are often powerful, it is a formal right to speak, even if the final decision stays with the government.
sawal: Who will be made responsible for getting the notice to the victim?
ref: Remission
The government's power to reduce or waive the rest of a convict's sentence and release them early.

h: New delimitation draft: an 850-seat Lok Sabha, frozen till 2051
dek: After the bill defeated in April, the government has put in writing a proposal to raise every state's seats by 50 percent, to be introduced on 30 November.
body: The central government has released the draft of the Constitution (132nd Amendment) Bill 2026. It proposes delimitation of constituencies based on the latest census. Every state's Lok Sabha and Assembly seats will rise by 50 percent, and the new boundaries will stay frozen until 2051. The maximum strength of the Lok Sabha will go from 550 to 850, the cap for states from 530 to 815, and for Union Territories from 20 to 35. The upper limit for Assemblies will rise from 500 to 650.

The bill also ties the 33 percent reservation for women to delimitation. Amit Shah has argued that 850 seats are needed so that after one-third go to women, the remaining seats stay close to the old number. In April the 131st Amendment Bill fell in the Lok Sabha, when 211 of the 489 members present voted against it. At that time an equal increase for every state was not in writing, only a verbal assurance.

The new bill is to come up at a special sitting of the Lok Sabha on 30 November and needs a two-thirds majority. According to the report, the DMK and NCP may support it, because a 50 percent increase and a 25-year freeze were their demands. Defections of MPs from the TMC, AAP and Shiv Sena (UBT) have also strengthened the NDA's numbers.
nazar: A written promise of an equal increase for every state calms the South's fears to some extent, but questions remain. Orders of the Delimitation Commission cannot be challenged in court, and the boundaries will be drawn under the watch of the same commission whose credibility is being questioned across the country today. Tying women's reservation once again to a long process is as good as putting it off.
sawal: Is a two-thirds majority gathered through defections enough to change the Constitution?
ref: Delimitation
Redrawing the boundaries and number of Lok Sabha and Assembly constituencies according to population. The number of seats has been frozen since 1976.

h: Three sanitation workers die in a septic tank in Hyderabad
dek: Two went down to save one, and none of the three came back; according to the Safai Karmachari Andolan, such deaths this year have crossed 138.
body: Three young workers died of toxic gas on Tuesday while cleaning the septic tank of an apartment complex in Bachupally, Hyderabad. The dead were K. Shanmukh Rao alias Suman (26), Suresh Gajiki (24) and Y. Pavan (20), all from villages in Andhra Pradesh's Srikakulam district. Police have registered a case of culpable homicide not amounting to murder against Ravi, owner of the company that hired them. He is accused of providing neither safety equipment nor any supervision.

According to the complaint by a relative of Suresh, Suman suddenly fainted while working in the tank. Pavan went in to save him and he too lost consciousness. Then Suresh went to check on the two, but none of the three came out.

Bezwada Wilson, national convenor of the Safai Karmachari Andolan, said that with these deaths, the number of people who died in sewers and septic tanks in the country this year has gone above 138, and governments are silent about it. The 2013 law bans employing people in such hazardous work. The Andolan alleges that 593 people died between January 2021 and July 2026, while the government told Parliament there were 332 deaths.
nazar: This is not an accident but a crime that is repeated every week even after law upon law has been made. Those who die are almost always poor, migrant and mostly Dalit, and accountability stops at the contractor. Until machines arrive and action is also taken against the housing societies that hand out the contracts, these numbers will keep rising.
sawal: Why are 261 deaths missing from the government's figures?
ref: Prohibition of Manual Scavengers Act 2013
A law that bans employing people to clean human excreta by hand or to clean sewers and septic tanks without protection, and also provides for rehabilitation.

h: Garbage piles up on Pampore's saffron fields, NGT orders a probe
dek: On a petition by 37 farmers, the tribunal has formed a joint committee that must report in eight weeks.
body: The National Green Tribunal (NGT) has formed a joint committee to look into the dumping of municipal waste near saffron fields in Pampore, Kashmir, and it must report in eight weeks. The order came at the first hearing of a petition by 37 farmers and environmental activist Raja Muzaffar Bhat. The petitioners want the dump site closed and the farmers compensated. The committee will also include a scientist from the Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences.

According to the people of Patalbagh village, Pampore town's waste has been dumped on about eight acres of land since 2022, and roughly 50 small trucks arrive every day. An inspection by the Jammu and Kashmir Pollution Control Committee found mixed waste and dirty water leaking from it. The committee's regional director has called this landfill illegal.

Down To Earth visited the area in August and found that many farmers had given up growing saffron because of a plague of rats. The rats dig burrows in the fields and damage the saffron corms and the flowering stage. Bhat estimates that 200 to 250 acres of saffron fields have been ruined. The next hearing is on 3 February 2027.
nazar: Pampore's saffron is Kashmir's identity and the livelihood of thousands of families, and to save it the farmers had to go from officials' doors all the way to the tribunal. Dumping a town's waste on a village's fertile land is an old disease of urban planning. Now we will see whether, after eight weeks, the garbage goes along with the report.
sawal: How did an illegal landfill keep running for four years?
ref: NGT
The National Green Tribunal, a special court set up in 2010 that hears environmental disputes and can order compensation.

h: New survey finds 56% of women anaemic
dek: The government is calling ICMR's SAMPADA survey an improvement, but experts say it is wrong to measure it against the NFHS, and only half the scheme's money was spent.
body: On 24 November the central government released the anaemia figures from ICMR's SAMPADA 2023-25 survey. According to them, 56 percent of women aged 15 to 49, 46 percent of adolescent girls aged 10 to 19 and 42 percent of children aged 12 to 59 months have anaemia. The NFHS-6 factsheet released in May did not have an anaemia figure at all, for the first time since 1992-93. This report first appeared in The News Minute.

The Health Ministry is comparing it with NFHS-5 and calling the 25.2-point fall among children a good sign. But the two surveys use different methods: SAMPADA took blood from a vein, the NFHS from a finger. The age definition of adolescents is also different, and SAMPADA's 1.7 lakh (170,000) samples are far fewer than NFHS-5's more than seven lakh (700,000) women. Public health expert Dr Sylvia Karpagam says removing the anaemia figure from the NFHS was deliberate.

The Anaemia Mukt Bharat (Anaemia-free India) scheme, launched in 2018, has not spent its money in full either. According to a Lok Sabha reply in March 2026, average use was 52.82 percent, and in 2024-25 only 38.93 percent of Rs 809 crore was spent. The gap between the amounts sanctioned and spent is Rs 2,264 crore.
nazar: Anaemia in more than half of all women is a national crisis by any measure, whether the sample is taken from a finger or a vein. Showing a fall by changing the method, and dropping the figure from the old survey altogether, creates doubt, not trust. A scheme with half its money lying unspent should give an account before claiming success.
sawal: Whose decision was it to drop the anaemia figure from NFHS-6?
ref: NFHS
The National Family Health Survey, the country's largest household health survey, carried out since 1992-93.
SAMPADA
ICMR's 2023-25 survey that recorded the population's health, diet and body measurements.

h: Siang dam opponents Ebo Mili and Otul Jerang freed after a month
dek: In the case over the 23 October protests in Pasighat, the East Siang sessions court granted bail to the human rights lawyer and the activist.
body: Arunachal Pradesh human rights lawyer Ebo Mili and activist Otul Jerang were released from jail on bail on Thursday. The two had surrendered at Pasighat police station on 27 October, after which they were arrested.

The case relates to the protests in Pasighat on 23 October against the proposed Siang Upper Multipurpose Project. Police registered several FIRs, with charges of unlawful assembly, rioting, obstructing government work, criminal conspiracy and damaging public property. One FIR accused a crowd of throwing stones and damaging an ambulance. District and Sessions Judge K. Taso said it mentions no serious injury to anyone, that it is at most a bailable offence, and that at first sight there is no evidence of the accused's role.

As a bail condition, Mili has been told not to take part in or call for any unlawful bandh (shutdown) or gathering. Mili and Jerang have already said the aim was to keep the movement peaceful and that they distance themselves from violence. The government calls the 11,000 megawatt dam essential for national security as a response to China's dam, while local communities say it will destroy their land, river and forests.
nazar: Keeping a lawyer in jail for a month on an FIR that the judge himself called weak shows that the arrest was really the punishment. Silencing the voice of the Adi community in the name of national security will not make the question of the dam go away.
sawal: Who will answer for a month in jail on a weak FIR?
ref: Siang Upper Multipurpose Project
A proposed dam of about 11,000 megawatts on the Siang river in Arunachal, opposed by Adi community villages that fear displacement.
ask: Scrap the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project

h: Thousands of students march in Dhubri: stop evictions, resettle the uprooted
dek: The All Assam Minority Students' Union marched to the DC's office and sent a memorandum to the Chief Minister, demanding a halt to the proposed eviction at Chapar-Falimari.
body: In Dhubri, Assam, thousands of members of the All Assam Minority Students' Union (AAMSU) marched to the Deputy Commissioner's office on Friday. The organisation called it a protest against arbitrary and inhuman evictions and sent a memorandum to Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma through the Deputy Commissioner. The march was led by president Imtiaz Hussain, chief adviser Ainuddin Ahmed and general secretaries Minnatul Islam and Kuddus Ali Sarkar.

According to the memorandum, about 1,355 families were removed from government khas, patta (titled) and allotted land at Chirakuta-Charuabakhra. AAMSU alleges that four schools, four mosques, three graveyards, two Eidgahs and two anganwadi (childcare) centres were also demolished there. Hundreds of people are still living in makeshift tents without water, toilets or medical care, and a woman named Sakina Khatun has died in one camp. At Alamganj-Rangamati about 650 families were removed, many of whom had settled there five decades ago after being uprooted by river erosion.

Now about 2,000 families at Chapar-Falimari face the threat of eviction, of whom about 700 are said to hold pattas; more than 150 families in six villages have already received notices. The organisation has demanded a committee of officials and community representatives for a fair check of land records, compensation, pattas for the landless and immediate relief in the camps. The report carries no response from the government.
nazar: Uprooting families with bulldozers a second time, after the river already uprooted them once, is not governance, it is punishment. That even patta holders have received notices shows this drive runs less on records and more on identity.
sawal: On what basis are 700 families holding pattas called encroachers?
ref: Khas land
Government-owned land in Assam that is not recorded in anyone's name; many people uprooted by river erosion have lived on such land for decades.
ask: Stop the eviction drive at once and rehabilitate the displaced

h: Ten villages in Siddharthnagar: we will not give our fields for a corridor
dek: Farmers of Bansi tehsil allege that their two-crop land was surveyed without telling them; they reached the Collectorate to protest.
ask: Leave fertile fields alone, set up industry on barren government land
body: Farmers from about 10 villages of the Chhitauni nyay panchayat in Bansi tehsil of Siddharthnagar district reached the Collectorate on Friday. They fear their farmland will be taken for UPSIDA's industrial corridor and factories. The farmers met the Additional District Magistrate to put their case and handed a memorandum to the District Magistrate.

The farmers say they learnt of the plan only when lekhpals (village land record officials), who had come to check tubewells and borings, told them the fields were being surveyed. They allege the survey was done without their knowledge or consent. Kewal Bahan Chaudhary of Chhitauni village in the Manikaura Nankar gram panchayat said the villagers have still not received any clear official notice about the project.

The farmers say this land is very fertile, gives two crops a year, and for many families it is the only farmland they have. They demand that fertile fields be kept out of the acquisition, that the industrial area be built on barren, fallow or empty government land, and that affected farmers be consulted before so big a decision is taken. The farmers made it clear they are not against industry, but they will not give up the land that feeds them. The report does not record any response from the administration.
nazar: That a farmer should hear of a survey of his own land through a lekhpal's chatter is an open violation of the spirit of the 2013 land acquisition law. The first step of development should be consent, not measuring tape.
sawal: On whose orders were the fields surveyed without telling the farmers?
ref: UPSIDA
The Uttar Pradesh State Industrial Development Authority, which acquires and develops land for industrial areas and corridors in the state.
Land Acquisition Act 2013
Under it, a social impact assessment and, for private projects, the consent of affected families are mandatory.

h: Foundation Day date shifted, Adivasi groups call a Jharkhand bandh
dek: Organisations called the decision to hold the 15 November celebration on 28 November, along with the government's anniversary, an insult to Birsa Munda and the movement's fighters.
body: Several Adivasi (indigenous) organisations in Jharkhand and groups linked to the Jharkhand movement have called a statewide bandh (shutdown) on Saturday, 28 November. Their anger is over the main celebration of the state's 26th Foundation Day, put off from 15 November because of Chhath, which will now be held on 28 November at Khelgaon in Ranchi along with the government's second anniversary.

Jharkhand was formed on 15 November 2000, the birth anniversary of Birsa Munda. Leaders of the organisations say changing the date lowers the historic importance of the Jharkhand movement, ignores the sacrifices of its fighters and disrespects Birsa Munda. Those calling the bandh include the Jharkhand Andolankari Morcha, Adivasi Bachao Yuva Morcha, Adivasi Jan Parishad, Adivasi Chhatra Sangh and Raji Padha Sarna Prarthana Sabha. Leaders such as Premshahi Munda, Sita Kachhap and Akash Tirkey are busy with preparations.

The bandh strategy was drawn up at a meeting at the Sirmatoli central Sarna site in Ranchi, and on Wednesday evening a torch procession went from Jaipal Singh Stadium to Albert Ekka Chowk. More protests are planned for 27 November. The organisations have sought support from traders, transporters and ordinary people. No official guidelines on schools, markets and buses have come so far. The report records no response from the government.
nazar: A date may seem a small thing, but in a state whose very identity was built by Birsa Munda and the movement for a separate state, merging Foundation Day into a government celebration puts Adivasi memory beneath the anniversary of those in power. That is what the organisations are angry about.
sawal: Why was it necessary to tie Foundation Day to the government's anniversary?
ref: Birsa Munda
The Munda hero who led the Ulgulan (great uprising) against the British and landlords in the late 19th century; Jharkhand was formed on his birth anniversary, 15 November.
Sarna
The nature-worshipping religious tradition of Jharkhand's Adivasis, and their sacred places of worship.

h: Bastar farmers to block the highway on 11 December for compensation
dek: Farmers from villages along the Narangi river have demanded relief of 65,100 rupees an acre for ruined crops.
ask: Compensation of 65,100 rupees an acre for crops destroyed by floods
body: In Chhattisgarh's Bastar division, heavy rain and floods ruined paddy, maize and vegetable crops ready for harvest in thousands of fields. Angry at not getting compensation, farmers at a meeting of the Kisan Sangharsh Samiti decided unanimously to hold a complete chakkajam (road blockade) on National Highway 63 on 11 December.

The farmers want relief of 65,100 rupees an acre. The movement includes farmers from villages on the banks of the Narangi river such as Belgaon, Bajawand, Bhejapadar, Bodra and Narayanpal, and the samiti is trying to bring together farmers from the whole area hit by the river.

The farmers had handed a memorandum to administrative officials on 6 November. They say the officers promised to take the demand to the state government, but three weeks later no real relief has come. Now the farmers have warned that if needed they will sit in an indefinite dharna (sit-in) on the highway itself, cooking and sleeping there. They say the movement will not stop until compensation is paid. The report records no statement from the government or the administration.
nazar: A survey and compensation after a flood are the basic duty of the administration, not a favour to farmers. When a memorandum lies in files for three weeks, lighting a stove on the highway is the only road left.
sawal: Why have Bastar's farmers got no relief even after three weeks?
ref: Chakkajam
A protest that completely stops vehicles on a road, an old method of farmers' movements.

h: Farmer-student march stopped on Mandir Marg in Delhi on Constitution Day
dek: The Samyukt Kisan Morcha gave memorandums addressed to the President at about 100 places, while Delhi Police invoked Section 163 and kept the road to Jantar Mantar shut.
ask: A legal guarantee of MSP, and the written promises of 2021 fulfilled
body: On Constitution Day, 26 November, the Samyukt Kisan Morcha sent a charter of demands to President Droupadi Murmu through District Magistrates at about 100 places across the country. The demands include a legal guarantee of MSP (minimum support price), action on the government's written assurances of 9 December 2021, a complete loan waiver, compensation of 25 lakh rupees to the families of farmers and farm workers who died by suicide, and a government insurance corporation in place of the crop insurance scheme. The Morcha also opposed the India-US trade deal and the SIR.

In Delhi, the farmers' front, farm workers' unions and left student groups including AISA were to march at 1 pm from Kali Bari on Mandir Marg to Jantar Mantar. Police said no application had been received, so permission was not given, and the Deputy Commissioner's notice cited prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita. According to the report, the protesters were stopped on Mandir Marg itself, and heavy police were deployed near the Laxminarayan temple.

The same day, farmers in Haryana gathered at Bahadurgarh planning to move towards the Tikri border, the Bharatiya Kisan Union in Punjab protested over sugarcane dues, and a rally on social justice and reservation was held at Ramabai Ambedkar Maidan in Lucknow. The report gives no crowd numbers for any place.
nazar: Blocking, on Constitution Day of all days, the right to peaceful assembly that the Constitution gives is a comment in itself. Instead of talking about the written promises to farmers, whose fifth anniversary is coming, barricades have become the answer in the capital.
sawal: By what logic is assembly banned on Constitution Day?
ref: Assurance of 9 December 2021
After the three farm laws were withdrawn, the Centre gave the farmers' front a written promise of a committee on MSP, withdrawal of cases and compensation.
Section 163, Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita
The provision that replaced the old Section 144, under which a magistrate can ban gatherings in an area.

h: Pineapples flourish in Niyamgiri, but the trader sets the price
dek: Dongria Kondh families of Khambesi village in Odisha grow plenty of pineapples on the hill slopes, but with no storage and no market the crop sells for a pittance.
body: In Khambesi village of Rayagada district, in July and August, pineapples are everywhere: on the slopes, in baskets on farmers' heads and in heaps outside homes. The Dongria Kondh who live here are counted among the Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs), and their livelihood is tied to the Niyamgiri hills and forest. Along with pineapple they also grow turmeric, ginger, arhar (pigeon pea) and mandia (finger millet).

Thirty-eight-year-old Mishra Kadraka looks after five thousand plants of the Simachal variety on about ten acres. He says this farming needs neither fertiliser nor pesticide, only hard work by hand, and the women of the house work equally in the orchard. At harvest, outside labourers have to be hired to bring the fruit down the slope, and their wage works out to about three rupees a fruit.

The real trouble is the price. A big fruit sells for 15-20 rupees, a medium one for 8-12 and a small one for 5-7 rupees, and the cost of two or three rupees for plucking and carrying comes out of this. The nearest market, Chatikona, is ten kilometres away and the road is broken, so farmers depend on traders who come from Raipur and now even Mumbai. In the rains the fruit starts rotting in the open, so they have to accept whatever price they get.

Government efforts are on paper. The Dongria Kondh Development Agency and ORMAS built a cold storage and processing unit at Chatikona in 2023-24, but in August 2026 the reporter found it deserted and shut. A new unit to make jam, jelly and squash is expected to start by 2027-28, and approval is still pending. Sarpanch Subardini Wadaka says the project is stuck for lack of money, while ripe fruit does not wait.

This is why pineapple does not run a household. Young men of the village, some only fourteen or fifteen, go to Kerala and Andhra to work as labourers, because there they get four to five hundred rupees a day and here two hundred.
nazar: Niyamgiri is the same hill the Dongria Kondh saved from mining. Now their fight is with the market, and in it the government's support is worth about as much as the shut cold storage. If farming that rests on the forest is to be saved, villages need storage nearby, a proper road and a guaranteed minimum price, or else the trader will take the profit and the children will leave for labour in other states.
sawal: Why has the Chatikona cold storage stayed shut after being built?
ref: Dongria Kondh
An Adivasi community living in Odisha's Niyamgiri hills, who regard the mountain as their god. In 2013 their gram sabhas (village assemblies) rejected Vedanta's bauxite mine.
PVTG
Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups: Adivasi communities with small populations, low literacy and livelihoods that rest on the forest. There are separate government schemes for them.

h: The fight for Tijmali: fake gram sabhas and arrests for bauxite
dek: Adivasis and Dalits opposing Vedanta's proposed bauxite mine in Odisha's Rayagada and Kalahandi are facing police raids, cases and allegations of a fake gram sabha.
body: On 16 October, doctor Randall Sequeira and activist Laxman Nayak were arrested in Bhawanipatna. Sequeira has been treating people in the area's villages since 2017, and they call him Doctor Dada. Police allege the two were inciting Adivasis.

The matter concerns the Sijimali mine lease given to Vedanta in 2023, under which about 31 crore (310 million) tonnes of bauxite are to be mined over 31 years. The mine will spread over 1,548 hectares and affect 44 villages. Naringidei Majhi, a Kondh Paroja farmer of Sagabari village, asks whether, if the hills and springs are gone, they should become labourers in the city. Bauxite hills soak up rain like a sponge and feed the springs, which means the mine will take the water too.

The area falls under the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution, where under the Forest Rights Act and PESA forest land cannot be handed over without the approval of the gram sabha (village assembly). Villagers allege that on 8 December 2023, in the presence of police, people brought from outside were seated to stage a Sagabari gram sabha. Papers obtained through RTI allegedly carry the signatures of people who are dead or have left the state. Vedanta says it had no role in these proceedings. In 2024 the villagers rejected those resolutions in their own gram sabhas and went to the High Court.

Despite this, in May 2026 forest clearance was given for a road to the mine, which has been challenged in the Green Tribunal. In April, after people stopped tree felling, police raided Kantamal at midnight. More than fifty people face FIRs, some under the UAPA too, and people complain of surveillance by drone.

Naringidei herself was arrested from a hospital in August 2025, while her grandson was being born. A condition to clean the police station was attached to her bail, which the Supreme Court struck down. The villagers call the grandson Sangram (struggle).
nazar: In Niyamgiri, real gram sabhas held on the Supreme Court's orders rejected Vedanta; in Tijmali, the allegation is that the gram sabha itself was hollowed out to escape that lesson. When a doctor who treats people and farmers who protest come within the net of an anti-terror law, the Fifth Schedule and PESA survive only in books. The court and the Green Tribunal should order an independent inquiry into the allegation of fake signatures.
sawal: Who will investigate a gram sabha signed by dead people?
ref: PESA Act
The Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996. In Fifth Schedule areas it gives the gram sabha the right to decide on land, forest and resources.
Niyamgiri verdict
In 2013 the Supreme Court said gram sabhas should decide on mining in Niyamgiri. All twelve gram sabhas rejected Vedanta's mine.

h: Three feet tall, full of courage: living with dwarfism in Bihar
dek: Golu of Buxar and Gautam and Soni of Nawada describe what school taunts, discrimination at home and the search for work are like with dwarfism, and why government entitlements do not reach them.
body: Twenty-one-year-old Golu Kumar Kushwaha of Buxar is under three feet tall and works as a mechanic in an e-rickshaw workshop. When he meets a new employer, he says: let me do the work first, and pay only if you like it, because people assume he cannot do anything. Now the e-rickshaw drivers respectfully call him Chhotu Bhaiya (little brother).

This respect did not come easily. Right after he was born, a neighbour advised his mother Sunita Devi to kill the baby by feeding him salt, which she refused. At the government school children kept teasing him as a dwarf and no teacher stopped them, so he left school in Class 8. When he was in Class 4, circus people came to buy him for five lakh rupees to make him a clown. The family said no, but for months his mother herself walked him to school and back.

While looking for work, shopkeepers turned him away on seeing his height. When he got a job delivering water, it paid fifteen hundred rupees a month. At last an e-rickshaw shop took him on trial, and in three years he learnt all the work just by watching. Today he pays for the coaching of his younger sister, who boxes. From the government he gets only a disability pension of 1,100 rupees, and he does not even know about reservation in government jobs.

In Qadirganj in Nawada district, Gautam Kumar Barnwal and his wife Soni are both short-statured. After the wedding Soni was mocked at her in-laws' home and Gautam was made to do heavy work, and then the family separated them, handing them a tiny grocery shop and a loan of seventy thousand. A cyber cafe owner wrongly told them that the pension is only for those under four feet, so they gave up on the application.
The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act of 2016 recognised dwarfism as a separate category, but the 2011 Census did not count such people separately, so nobody has the right number.
nazar: The law recognised dwarfism as a disability ten years ago, but the stories of Golu and Gautam show that the rights have not travelled from paper to the village. Stopping taunts in school, getting correct information on pensions and reservation to people, and counting them are the basic work of the government. For the boy who escaped a circus deal and became a mechanic by his own effort, the biggest barrier is society's staring eye.
sawal: Will the next Census count people with dwarfism separately?
ref: Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016
This law set out 21 categories of disability, including dwarfism. It provides for four per cent reservation for persons with disabilities in government jobs.

h: When prayer becomes a crime: the testimony of Adivasi Christians in Madhya Pradesh
dek: A team linked to Karwan-e-Mohabbat went to the Adivasi areas of Madhya Pradesh in May 2026 and recorded the testimony of about twenty-five people who faced violence driven by religious hatred; The Wire has released it.
body: This documentary on The Wire's YouTube channel is about rising violence against Christians in Madhya Pradesh, and its focus is on the people this violence falls on hardest: Christians from Adivasi (indigenous) communities. According to the film's introduction, a team linked to Karwan-e-Mohabbat went to the state's Adivasi areas in May 2026, recorded the testimony of victims and met villagers and community leaders.

The film rests on the words of about twenty-five victims from Jhabua, Alirajpur, Burhanpur, Khandwa, Bhopal and Mhow. Of these, Jhabua and Alirajpur are Bhil-majority districts of western Madhya Pradesh with a very large Adivasi population. The introduction says plainly that the aim is to give a voice to victims of violence driven by religious hatred, which means the story is told in their own words.

The film's title is its question: when does prayer become a crime? The background is familiar. Madhya Pradesh has had the Freedom of Religion Act in force since 2021, which makes conversion by force, lure or fraud a crime and requires notice to the district administration before changing religion. Civil rights groups have long said that under cover of such laws, police are called even to ordinary prayer meetings in homes on charges of conversion, and cases are filed against pastors and ordinary believers.

In Adivasi areas this conflict is tied to another question: are Adivasis who became Christian still Adivasi? Some organisations have been demanding that such people be removed from the Scheduled Tribes list, and this debate has driven a wedge between families and neighbours in many villages. The film comes against the backdrop of this climate.

Karwan-e-Mohabbat was started in 2017 by former IAS officer and writer Harsh Mander, when a journey set out to reach the families of people killed in mob violence. Since then the group has been meeting victims of hate violence, recording their accounts and taking them to people. The film is directed and shot by Imad Ul Hasan, Safa K.T. is also on camera, and it is edited by Vedant, Safa K.T., Hifzul Bahar and Imad Ul Hasan.
More than an investigation of any one incident, this film is a record of the shared experience of many people, and those speaking are the ones who went through the violence.
nazar: News of violence against Christians is often dealt with in a line or two, and when the victims are Adivasis it goes even more unheard. This film fills that gap: twenty-five testimonies make a pattern, not an exception. The Constitution gives every citizen the right to profess and practise their religion; if praying at home becomes a reason to be called to the police station, that right is hollowed out. The government should investigate these complaints fairly, and society should remember that Adivasi identity is neither smaller nor bigger than anyone's faith.
sawal: Why is no action taken against those who call the police on prayer meetings at home?
ref: Madhya Pradesh Freedom of Religion Act, 2021
A state law that makes conversion by force, lure or fraud a crime. Notice to the District Magistrate is required before changing religion.
Karwan-e-Mohabbat
A campaign started by Harsh Mander in 2017 that meets families who are victims of mob and hate violence and brings their accounts to light.

h: A letter to God, with questions for men
dek: Gosiya Bano's open letter asks how a woman's plea will reach God if the men who speak in the name of religion are the ones writing the verdicts.
body: This piece, published on Hindwi's blog Bela, is a letter written straight to God. The writer says she lays her complaint before Him in every sajda (prostration in prayer) and wants an answer, but fears the answer too may come in the same tone in which the men of the world speak. If that happens, she will have to accept that men have made themselves the voice of God.

A large part of the letter is about the maulvis and qaris (clerics and Quran reciters) who give sermons on women's rights after Friday prayers. According to the writer, these sermons begin with purdah and come to rest on the woman's body, and even the blame for a man's evil gaze is put on the woman. She asks why the burqa and the ghunghat (veil) cannot make a man's eye pure, and why the burden of honour rests on the woman's shoulders alone.

Then she lists the inequality inside the home: the mother's mourning when a daughter is born, the woman's wishes counting for nothing in marriage, the man freeing himself by saying talaq three times while a woman needs her husband's consent for khula. She calls halala a punishment forced on women. The blame for infertility too always falls on the woman.

The writer reminds us that men want a Fatima in their wives, but are not ready to become Ali themselves. At the end she asks God for a clear answer that cannot be changed, and signs the letter: a woman of the world You made.
nazar: This letter is not a revolt against religion but a question to those who have made themselves its contractors. Its strength is that it stands inside faith and asks where the difference between God and men lies. Even after a law on triple talaq, a woman's helplessness in halala, khula and household decisions remains as it was, and this voice rises from that reality.

It is also important that this voice not be made into a weapon to curse any community. Patriarchy speaks from the platform of every religion; Bano's question is the question of every woman whose decisions someone else writes.
sawal: When will women's voices be heard in the mosque sermon?
ref: Khula
Divorce at the wife's initiative in Islamic law. In common practice, the husband's consent or a qazi's ruling is considered necessary for it.
Halala
The condition that, to remarry the same husband after divorce, a woman must first marry someone else. Many Muslim women's groups have been demanding it be ended.

h: A mother carrying bricks and a severed hand: poems by Golendra Patel
dek: Eleven poems by Golendra Patel, a young poet from Chandauli, put the worker, the farmer and the humiliation of caste at the centre of the poem.
body: Sammukh has published eleven poems by Golendra Patel, a young poet from Chandauli in Uttar Pradesh. Patel, who studied Hindi at Banaras Hindu University, writes in both Hindi and Bhojpuri. The ground of these poems is the field, the brick kiln and the workers' basti (settlement), and most are open, long, unrhymed poems.

In the first poem the poet keeps listing scenes he has seen: an old man weeping outside the court, a labouring mother who feeds her child first and stays hungry herself, a farmer sowing seed in a dry field, police excesses. At the end he speaks of a future where a person's worth is set by compassion. The poem about clouds turns Kalidasa's Meghduta (The Cloud Messenger) upside down: here the one sending the message is not a yaksha but a farmer.

The most personal poem in the set is about the poet's mother, who was a brick-carrying labourer. Dust, sweat, cracked heels and a long list of tools tell in it a story of child labour and the double burden on women. The poem about the chokar litti (bran bread) makes the identity of the margins stand tall against caste humiliation and hunger.

The poem Thresher is about a labourer whose hand is cut off in the machine, and it questions the powerful in Delhi about the owner's indifference. There is a long prayer dedicated to Premchand, and the last poem, in rhyming couplets, remembers the Buddha and compassion against war. In between there are also short, tender poems about spring and the first rain.
nazar: In these poems labour is not a distant subject but the story of a home. The poet's mother's bricks and the hand cut off in the thresher challenge the Hindi poetry that often turns the farmer and worker into a symbol and leaves them there. Patel's strength lies in his concrete things: bran, chaff, tools.

The weakness is clear too. Many poems are longer than they need to be, and the Premchand poem gets buried under heavy Sanskritised words. Still, this voice should be heard, because it comes from the section that has been written about a great deal but has itself written little.
sawal: Who decides the compensation for a hand cut off in a thresher?
ref: Meghduta
Kalidasa's Sanskrit poem, in which an exiled yaksha sends a message to his wife through a cloud.
Litti
A food of eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar made of flour or bran and roasted on fire, long a mark of working households.

h: A hundred years of 'Oil!', a finger on capitalism's vein
dek: Tamlyn Avery says Upton Sinclair's novel sees oil as the grease on which the whole machine of capitalism runs.
body: In this article, which came to Scroll from The Conversation, Tamlyn Avery marks a hundred years of Upton Sinclair's novel 'Oil!' and calls it the most far-sighted anti-capitalist epic in American literature. It was serialised in 1926-27 in the communist paper The Daily Worker, and the 2007 film 'There Will Be Blood' was inspired by it. According to Avery, oil for Sinclair is what whaling is in 'Moby-Dick': the key to understanding the modern world.

Sinclair grew up from 1878 amid poverty and workers' struggles, wrote in socialist magazines and lost several elections as a socialist candidate. His 1906 novel 'The Jungle' was about the exploitation of migrant workers in Chicago's slaughterhouses, after which food safety laws were made in America. He saw literature as a weapon of class struggle.

The idea for 'Oil!' came in 1921, when a Shell well gushed near Long Beach and a frenzy of speculation spread. The story is of Bunny, son of a Los Angeles oil man, who grows up watching his father bribe officials. The use of a detective agency to break strikes and the grip of oil money on universities shake him from within. His friend Paul is a symbol of the awakening working class, and is sent to Russia so that the oil interests of American banks can be protected.

Avery recalls that in 1934, when Sinclair ran for governor, Hollywood made newsreels to campaign against him. Today the world burns about 10 crore (100 million) barrels of oil a day, and according to the writer this novel challenges us to imagine the end of capitalism.
nazar: A hundred years on, this novel still stings because its world is ours: corporate money buys even universities, newspapers and cinema, and in elections the media becomes one side's weapon. Seeing how mining, port and power contracts in India are gathered in a few business houses, Sinclair's question does not feel old.
In the age of the climate crisis, it is necessary to see oil not just as fuel but as a structure of power. That is the reason to read this book again.
sawal: What corporate money keeps our universities quiet?
ref: Upton Sinclair
American novelist and socialist (1878-1968), whose 'The Jungle' opened the way for food safety laws.
The Daily Worker
A paper linked to the Communist Party of the USA, in which 'Oil!' first appeared as a serial.
photo_note: Smoke from factory chimneys, a 1905 painting

h: A diary from the anda cell: Arun Ferreira's Qaid Ke Rang
dek: Seema Azad writes that if you want to see the real face of a state, read the diaries written from its prisons.
body: This article is the introduction to 'Qaid Ke Rang' (Colours of the Cage), the Hindi edition of Arun Ferreira's prison diary, written by social activist Seema Azad. Her argument is that the real character of a state shows where it keeps people locked up, and only political prisoners can give such accounts.

Ferreira was picked up from a railway station on 7 May 2007 and called a big Maoist leader. According to the writer, false cases were filed against him one after another, and at every release he was re-arrested right at the jail gate. He came out in December 2011, after four years and eight months, most of it spent in the solitude of the anda cell of Nagpur jail. In 2018 he went to jail again in the Bhima Koregaon case, got bail in 2023, and according to Azad the NIA still wants his bail cancelled.

The diary describes torture in police custody, the absurdity of narco and polygraph tests, and evidence fabricated against innocent people. Azad notes that the same 'expert' officer appears in Abdul Wahid Shaikh's prison diary too. Ferreira also writes about the large number of Muslims in jails, the very low conviction rate in cases of atrocities against Dalits, and his own hunger strike against gate arrests.

Each chapter begins with a letter written from jail and a sketch by Ferreira. He did an MA in human rights in jail and started practising law after coming out. At the end Azad, herself a former political prisoner, recalls Ferreira saying that in his lonely cell he envied the collective life of ants.
nazar: Prison writing is becoming the most important record of our time, because under laws like the UAPA the trial itself has become the punishment. Ferreira's acquittal, and then his going to jail years later in another case, shows that the process is the punishment. The same officer appearing in the diaries of two different prisoners is no coincidence; it points to a system.
It matters that this book has come out in Hindi, because this is the language of the regions with the most undertrial prisoners.
sawal: Why do courts not stop re-arrests at the jail gate?
ref: Anda cell
The egg-shaped high-security section of Nagpur Central Jail, where prisoners are kept in long solitary confinement.
Bhima Koregaon case
A case registered after the 2018 violence, in which several lawyers, writers and activists were arrested under the UAPA.

h: Who defeated 1857: British cannon or our own informers?
dek: Shamsul Islam's book uses spies' letters to show how big a hand informing had in the defeat of the Ghadar (the 1857 revolt).
body: Faiyaz Ahmad Wajeeh, executive editor of The Wire Urdu, has reviewed historian Shamsul Islam's book '1857 Ghadar Ke Mukhbir: Jasoosoan Ke Khat' (Informers of the 1857 Revolt: Letters of Spies). Shamsul Islam is known for his work on nationalism and communalism. In this book he has gathered the letters that carried news of the rebels in Delhi to the British.

According to the reviewer, popular history puts the defeat of the revolt down to the skill of the British army and the fate of Indians, and calls the rebels looters. This book breaks that myth and shows that informing and betrayal played a big part in deciding the outcome. Wajeeh also asks why Sir Syed Ahmad Khan called rebels from lower castes looters: out of caste prejudice, or out of loyalty to the British.

According to the author, he found one bundle of letters among footpath books in Lahore's Anarkali Bazaar, while the larger collection is in London's India Office Library. In Urdu, Saleem Qureshi had worked on them earlier. The letters date from June to September 1857. One letter mentions about four hundred jihadis who came from Gwalior, and Hindu and Muslim fighters who swore on their own holy books.

The book divides the informers into three groups: soldiers sent among the rebels, harkaras (runners) who passed on news for a little money, and the most dangerous, Indians loyal to the British. The Urdu letters were translated into English at the Ambala headquarters and turned into reports. Shamsul Islam estimates that the anonymous letters came from people of well-known families.
nazar: This book comes at a time when history is being turned into a story of one religion's bravery and another's betrayal. The spies' letters show that in 1857 Hindus and Muslims fought together, and that betrayal belonged to no single community but grew out of the loyalty of powerful classes.
The reviewer's question is fair: why, even after a century and a half, have these documents not reached the ordinary reader and the syllabus?
sawal: Why are the real testimonies of 1857 not in the syllabus?
ref: Shamsul Islam
A historian who has taught political science at Delhi University and has written on nationalism, the RSS and 1857.
India Office Library
A collection of British Raj documents in London, now part of the British Library.
photo_note: A camel rider beating a nagara (kettledrum)

h: Anger is a woman's right: thirteen women, thirteen fights
dek: According to Saloni Sharma, Nilanjana Bhowmick's book sees a woman's anger not as madness but as a force for change.
body: In Scroll, Saloni Sharma reviews journalist Nilanjana Bhowmick's book 'Why the World Needs Angry Women' (Aleph). It begins with the point that anger was never considered a woman's to have. An angry woman is called hysterical, ugly and out of control; in myths she becomes a demoness, and in real life she faces trolling, exclusion and violence.

The book's thirteen chapters are on thirteen women who turned anger into change. The reviewer places it in the tradition of Mary Wollstonecraft, Sylvia Plath, Mahasweta Devi and Audre Lorde. Each chapter starts with a personal story and goes on to a critique of the exclusion of a whole community, keeping caste, class and place in mind.

Among them is Dalit human rights activist Beena Pallical, who learnt of her caste late and says that silence too keeps caste alive. Rituparna Borah of the queer feminist group Nazariya describes the family as a place of control and seeks legal recognition for chosen families. The fight of Fatima Nafees, mother of missing JNU student Najeeb Ahmed, who was targeted in the 2022 Bulli Bai episode, is here too.

The book also has Pallavi Pareek, fighting harassment at the workplace; Laxmi Kushwaha, a jal saheli (water friend) saving water in Bundelkhand; Sohini Chakraborty of Kolkata Sanved, who works through dance with women rescued from trafficking; and several artists. According to the reviewer, these stories make a picture of an Indian feminism resting not on noise but on repair and work.
nazar: In a country where a woman who asks questions is cornered first over her character and then on social media, justifying anger is a political act in itself. Fatima Nafees's name on this list is a reminder that Najeeb's question remains unresolved to this day.

The good thing about the book is that it keeps Dalit, queer, Muslim and village women together. From the review, though, it does seem that its emphasis is more on individual success and less on collective movements that take on structures.
sawal: Why does the anger of Najeeb Ahmed's mother frighten those in power?
ref: Audre Lorde
Black American feminist poet (1934-1992), whose 1981 essay 'The Uses of Anger' sees anger as a force for change.
Bulli Bai episode
A 2022 case in which photos of Muslim women were put up for 'auction' on an app, targeting several journalists and activists.
